chapters.summary: Cost accounting ascertains, records and controls cost. It is distinguished from financial accounting by purpose, periodicity and format, and from management accounting by scope. Cost classification is the prerequisite for every later chapter.

keyTerms.definition: Anything for which a separate measurement of cost is required — a product, service, department, customer or project.
A location, person or item of equipment for which costs may be ascertained and used for control; may be production or service.
A unit of product or service in relation to which costs are expressed — per tonne, per machine hour, per passenger-km.
Control maintains costs within predetermined standards; reduction achieves a permanent, genuine decrease in unit cost without impairing quality.
ICMAI-issued standards that standardise cost classification, measurement and presentation for cost records and cost audit.

formulas.name: Cost sheet build-up
formulas.expression: Prime cost = Direct material + Direct labour + Direct expenses | Works cost = Prime cost + Factory overheads ± WIP | Cost of production = Works cost + Administration overheads ± Finished stock | Cost of sales = Cost of production + Selling and distribution overheads | Sales − Cost of sales = Profit
formulas.meaning: The single most used structure in the paper; learn the exact sequence and the WIP/stock adjustments.

questions.q: Distinguish between cost accounting and management accounting.
questions.answer: Cost accounting records and ascertains cost of products and services, using historical and predetermined data, with statutory cost-record obligations for specified industries. Management accounting uses financial and cost data plus other information to assist management decisions, planning and control; it is broader, forward-looking and has no statutory format. Cost accounting is a subset of the information base that management accounting draws upon.

pitfalls: Adding administration overheads before factory overheads in the cost sheet sequence.
Treating abnormal loss as part of works cost.

chapters.summary: Elements of cost — material, labour and overheads — with their control techniques and valuation methods. This is the highest-frequency numerical block in the paper, covering EOQ, stock valuation, labour remuneration and overhead absorption.

keyTerms.definition: The order quantity at which the total of ordering cost and carrying cost is minimum.
The inventory level at which a fresh order must be placed, allowing for lead time and maximum consumption.
Classification of inventory by value and usage — A items high value/low quantity, C items low value/high quantity — to focus control effort.
Classification by criticality — Vital, Essential, Desirable — used for spares control.
Time lost by workers for which wages are paid but no production results; normal idle time is treated as part of labour cost, abnormal idle time is charged to the costing P&L.
Where absorbed overheads exceed actual overheads; the difference is a credit to the costing P&L.
Apportionment of service department costs where departments serve each other, using repeated distribution, simultaneous equations or the trial and error method.

formulas.name: Economic Order Quantity
formulas.expression: EOQ = √(2 × Annual consumption × Cost per order / Carrying cost per unit per annum)
formulas.meaning: At EOQ, ordering cost equals carrying cost.
formulas.example: Annual consumption 24,000 units; ordering cost ₹150; carrying cost ₹4/unit → EOQ = √(2×24,000×150/4) = √18,00,000 = 1,342 units.

formulas.name: Reorder level
formulas.expression: Reorder level = Maximum consumption × Maximum lead time
formulas.meaning: Triggers a new order before stock-out.
formulas.example: Maximum consumption 300 units/week, maximum lead time 4 weeks → 1,200 units.

formulas.name: Maximum and minimum level
formulas.expression: Maximum = Reorder level + EOQ − (Minimum consumption × Minimum lead time); Minimum = Reorder level − (Normal consumption × Normal lead time)
formulas.meaning: Used with average stock and danger level computations.
formulas.example: ROL 1,200, EOQ 1,342, min consumption 100, min lead time 2 → maximum 3,342; normal consumption 200, normal lead time 3 → minimum 600.

formulas.name: FIFO / weighted average issue price
formulas.expression: Weighted average = Total cost of materials in stock / Total quantity in stock
formulas.meaning: Recalculated after each receipt; smooths price fluctuations.
formulas.example: 1,000 units at ₹10 and 2,000 at ₹13 → weighted average ₹12.

formulas.name: Labour turnover
formulas.expression: Separation method = Separations / Average workers × 100; Replacement method = Replacements / Average workers × 100
formulas.meaning: Replacement method excludes new posts and is the better cost indicator.

formulas.name: Halsey and Rowan premium
formulas.expression: Halsey: earnings = Time taken × Rate + 50% × Time saved × Rate. Rowan: earnings = Time taken × Rate + (Time saved / Time allowed) × Time taken × Rate
formulas.meaning: Both share the benefit of time saved between worker and employer.

formulas.name: Machine hour rate
formulas.expression: Rate = (Fixed costs attributable to the machine + Variable running costs) / Machine hours
formulas.meaning: Used for absorption in a machine-intensive department.
formulas.example: Standing charges ₹1,20,000 + running ₹60,000 over 1,800 hours → ₹100 per machine hour.

formulas.name: Under/over absorption
formulas.expression: Absorbed = Actual hours × Predetermined rate; Variance = Absorbed − Actual overheads
formulas.meaning: Positive is over-absorption, negative is under-absorption.

examples.title: Repeated distribution of reciprocal service departments
examples.scenario: Service departments X and Y serve each other: X's costs ₹40,000, of which 20% goes to Y; Y's costs ₹30,000, of which 10% goes to X.
steps: Distribute X: 20% of 40,000 = 8,000 to Y; 80% to production.
Distribute Y (now 38,000): 10% = 3,800 to X; 90% to production.
Distribute X again (3,800): 20% = 760 to Y, balance to production. Continue until the residual is immaterial.
Alternatively solve the simultaneous equations X = 40,000 + 0.10Y and Y = 30,000 + 0.20X.
examples.result: X = 44,184 and Y = 38,837 approximately. State the method used — repeated, algebraic, or trial and error.

questions.q: Annual consumption 36,000 units; ordering cost ₹200 per order; carrying cost 20% of the unit price of ₹50. Compute EOQ and the number of orders per year.
questions.answer: Carrying cost per unit = 20% × 50 = ₹10. EOQ = √(2 × 36,000 × 200 / 10) = √14,40,000 = 1,200 units. Number of orders = 36,000/1,200 = 30 per year. Frequency approximately every 12 days.

questions.q: A worker is paid ₹120 per hour. Time allowed 50 hours, time taken 40 hours. Compute earnings under Halsey (50%) and Rowan.
questions.answer: Time saved = 10 hours. Halsey = 40 × 120 + 50% × 10 × 120 = 4,800 + 600 = ₹5,400. Rowan = 40 × 120 + (10/50) × 4,800 = 4,800 + 960 = ₹5,760. Rowan gives a higher incentive when the time saved is a small fraction of time allowed.

questions.q: Explain the treatment of normal and abnormal idle time.
questions.answer: Normal idle time is unavoidable and inherent in the process (waiting for work, machine setting, rest) and is treated as part of the cost of labour and absorbed into production by inflating the effective wage rate. Abnormal idle time arises from avoidable causes (power failure, strike, machine breakdown, shortage of materials) and is excluded from product cost, being charged to the costing profit and loss account so that product costs are not distorted.

questions.q: Overheads absorbed ₹6,80,000 against actual overheads of ₹6,35,000. Explain the treatment of the difference.
questions.answer: Over-absorption of ₹45,000. If the amount is small, credit it to the costing P&L account. If material, apportion it between work-in-progress, finished goods and cost of sales on an appropriate basis so that stock and cost of sales are stated correctly.

pitfalls: Using the annual carrying cost instead of the per-unit carrying cost in EOQ.
Charging abnormal idle time and abnormal wastage to product cost.
Forgetting the balance in the WIP account when computing works cost.

chapters.summary: The 24 Cost Accounting Standards standardise cost classification, measurement, attribution and presentation. Learn each as: scope → treatment → disclosure, since CAS questions are usually short theory.

keyTerms.definition: Cost is classified by nature, behaviour, function, traceability and relevance for decision-making.
Installed capacity, normal capacity and actual capacity; definitions for cost records.
Collection, allocation, apportionment and absorption of overheads, including treatment of under/over absorption.

keyTerms.term: CAS 4 — Cost of Production / Cost of Sales / Cost of Services
keyTerms.definition: Defines the components and the order in which they are aggregated.
Method for averaging freight cost where the same rate is charged to all customers.
Treatment of captive power, steam and water costs.

keyTerms.term: CAS 13 — Cost of Service Cost Centre
keyTerms.definition: Treatment of service cost centres whose output is not measurable in units.
Classification of prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs.

keyTerms.term: CAS 24 — Treatment of Revenue in Cost Statements
keyTerms.definition: Treatment of discounts, subsidies and other revenue items in cost statements.

revisionNotes: Learn the CAS number → title mapping; examiners ask 'state the treatment of X under CAS Y'.
CAS 3 is the backbone of overhead questions; CAS 4 gives the definitive cost sheet sequence.
Joint costs and by-products are covered by CAS 19; abnormal costs by CAS 23.

chapters.summary: Cost bookkeeping uses a double-entry system with control accounts for materials, labour and overheads. Integral accounting merges cost and financial ledgers; non-integral accounting keeps them separate and requires reconciliation.

keyTerms.definition: A single set of books in which cost and financial transactions are recorded together, with cost ledgers integrated into the financial ledgers.
Separate cost and financial books, linked by a cost ledger control account and periodic reconciliation.
In non-integral books, the account that represents the financial ledger and balances the cost ledger.
Items included in cost accounts that have no counterpart in financial accounts — notional rent, notional interest on capital, notional salary to the proprietor.

formulas.name: Reconciliation statement
formulas.expression: Profit as per cost accounts ± Items in cost only ∓ Items in financial only ± Over/under absorption ± Stock valuation differences = Profit as per financial accounts
formulas.meaning: Explain each difference by its cause, not just its amount.
formulas.example: Cost profit ₹5,00,000 + notional rent ₹40,000 − over-absorbed overheads ₹15,000 + dividend received ₹25,000 = financial profit ₹5,50,000.

questions.q: State any six reasons for the difference between profit as per cost accounts and as per financial accounts.
questions.answer: (i) Items included only in financial accounts, such as dividends, interest, donations and loss on sale of assets; (ii) items included only in cost accounts, such as notional rent, notional interest and imputed salary; (iii) different valuation of closing stock — cost or market price versus cost only; (iv) different depreciation methods or rates; (v) over- or under-absorption of overheads; (vi) abnormal losses treated differently; (vii) differences in the basis of apportionment of common costs; (viii) notional transfer pricing between departments.

pitfalls: Adding a cost-only item when reconciling from cost profit to financial profit — check the direction of each adjustment.

chapters.summary: Job, batch and contract costing are specific-order methods. Contract costing adds work certified, retention, escalation and profit recognition on incomplete contracts.

keyTerms.definition: Costs are collected against each separately identifiable job or customer order.
Costs are collected per batch; unit cost = batch cost / number of units, with EBQ as the economic batch quantity.
A form of job costing for long-term, site-based contracts where costs are accumulated against the contract.
Value of work completed and approved by the customer's engineer; determines the amount billable.
A percentage withheld by the customer until completion or a defect-liability period.
A contract provision raising the price if material or labour costs rise beyond an agreed limit.
Value of work certified plus work uncertified minus cost incurred to date.

formulas.name: Notional profit
formulas.expression: Notional profit = Work certified + Work uncertified − Cost incurred to date
formulas.meaning: A progress measure before applying the recognition rule.

formulas.name: Profit to be transferred — below 25%
formulas.expression: No profit is credited to the P&L
formulas.meaning: Conservatism: early-stage contracts carry no profit.

formulas.name: Profit to be transferred — 25% to 50%
formulas.expression: Profit transferred = Notional profit × 1/3 × Cash received / Work certified
formulas.meaning: One-third rule where cash collection is a constraint.

formulas.name: Profit to be transferred — above 50%
formulas.expression: Profit transferred = Notional profit × 2/3 × Cash received / Work certified
formulas.meaning: Two-thirds rule; the balance is carried as a reserve.

formulas.name: Estimated total profit
formulas.expression: Total profit = Contract price − Estimated total cost; current year's transfer = Total profit × Work certified / Contract price (for fixed-price contracts)
formulas.meaning: Used where the contract is near completion and total cost can be reliably estimated.
formulas.example: Price ₹50,00,000, estimated cost ₹44,00,000 → profit ₹6,00,000; 60% certified → ₹3,60,000 × cash ratio.

examples.title: Contract profit recognition
examples.scenario: Contract price ₹40,00,000. Cost incurred ₹16,00,000. Work certified ₹18,00,000, uncertified ₹80,000. Cash received ₹16,20,000.
steps: Completion by work certified = 45%, which is in the 25–50% band.
examples.result: Credit ₹84,000 to the P&L; the balance is a reserve in WIP.

questions.q: A contract has a price of ₹60,00,000; cost incurred ₹24,00,000; work certified ₹26,00,000; cash received 90%. Compute the profit to be transferred.
questions.answer: Notional profit = 26,00,000 − 24,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. Work certified/price = 43.3% → 25–50% band → transfer 1/3 × 2,00,000 × 0.90 = ₹60,000 to the P&L and carry forward ₹1,40,000 as reserve.

questions.q: Distinguish between work certified and work uncertified and explain why uncertified work is valued at cost.
questions.answer: Work certified is work completed and approved by the customer's architect or engineer, and is the basis for billing and progress payments. Work uncertified is work done but not yet approved at the reporting date. It is valued at cost (excluding profit) because the contractor has not yet earned the right to payment, and recognising profit on it would breach prudence.

pitfalls: Recognising profit on uncertified work.
Forgetting to deduct retention money when computing cash received.
Using the total estimated cost instead of the cost incurred to date in the notional profit computation.

chapters.summary: Process costing applies to continuous production. The central skills are equivalent production, normal and abnormal loss, inter-process profit elimination, and apportioning joint costs between joint products and by-products.

keyTerms.definition: Expressing partly completed units in terms of completed units — units × percentage of completion — to apportion costs between finished output and WIP.
Unavoidable loss inherent in the process, often expressed as a percentage of input; its scrap value reduces the cost of the process.
Loss above normal; valued at the normal cost per unit and charged to the costing P&L.
Where actual loss is less than normal; valued at normal cost and credited to the costing P&L.
Profit included in the transfer price between processes that remains unrealised in closing stock and must be eliminated through a reserve.
Products of similar value produced simultaneously from the same process up to the split-off point.
A product of comparatively small value produced incidentally; its revenue reduces the cost of the main product.

formulas.name: Normal cost per unit
formulas.expression: Normal cost per unit = (Total process cost − Scrap value of normal loss) / (Input units − Normal loss units)
formulas.meaning: Used to value abnormal loss and abnormal gain and to price good output.
formulas.example: Cost ₹1,00,000; input 1,000; normal loss 10% with scrap ₹5 → (1,00,000 − 500)/900 = ₹110.56 per unit.

formulas.name: Abnormal loss value
formulas.expression: Abnormal loss = Abnormal loss units × Normal cost per unit
formulas.meaning: Plus any recovery, the balance is charged to the P&L.

formulas.name: Equivalent production — weighted average
formulas.expression: Equivalent units = Units completed and transferred + Closing WIP × Degree of completion + Normal loss (if fully complete)
formulas.meaning: Opening WIP is already included in the cost pool under weighted average.

formulas.name: Joint cost apportionment
formulas.expression: Physical units method | Market value at split-off | Net realisable value | Standard cost method
formulas.meaning: Choose the method that reflects benefit received; NRV is preferred where products require further processing.

formulas.name: Inter-process profit reserve
formulas.expression: Reserve on closing stock = (Transfer price − Cost) × Closing stock / Units transferred
formulas.meaning: Deduct from the transferring process's profit; carry forward as a stock reserve.
formulas.example: Profit loaded ₹20/unit, closing stock 200 of 1,000 transferred → reserve ₹4,000.

examples.title: Abnormal loss and gain together
examples.scenario: Process input 2,000 units at ₹50,000; normal loss 10% with scrap value ₹2/unit; actual output 1,850 units; process expenses ₹20,000.
steps: Actual output 1,850 means loss was 150 units — 50 units less than normal → abnormal gain of 50 units.
Abnormal gain = 50 × 38.67 = ₹1,933, credited to the P&L.
examples.result: Cost of good output = 1,850 × 38.67 = ₹71,533, and the process account balances.

questions.q: Input 4,000 units costing ₹1,20,000; normal loss 5%; scrap value of normal loss ₹10 per unit; output 3,700 units. Compute the normal cost per unit and the abnormal loss.
questions.answer: Normal loss = 200 units, scrap ₹2,000. Normal cost = (1,20,000 − 2,000)/3,800 = ₹31.05 per unit. Actual loss = 300 units, abnormal loss = 100 units valued at ₹3,105, charged to the costing P&L. Cost of output = 3,700 × 31.05 = ₹1,14,895.

questions.q: Explain why inter-process profit is eliminated and how.
questions.answer: Where a process transfers its output to the next process at cost plus a profit margin, part of that internal profit remains unrealised in closing stock at the year end. Recognising it would overstate profit, because no sale to an external party has occurred. The unrealised element is computed by comparing the transfer price with the actual cost of the units in closing stock, and is eliminated by crediting a stock reserve in the transferring process account and carrying the reserve in the balance sheet. In the final process, all internal profit is realised on sale and no reserve is needed.

pitfalls: Including normal loss units in equivalent production where the loss has no scrap value.
Forgetting to eliminate inter-process profit in closing stock.
Valuing abnormal gain at selling price instead of normal cost.

chapters.summary: Operating costing applies to service organisations where a composite cost unit is used — per passenger-km, per tonne-km, per bed-day, per patient-day, per room-night.

keyTerms.definition: A method of costing used for services where the product is not tangible and cost is expressed per unit of service.
A unit combining two measures, such as tonne-kilometre or passenger-kilometre.
Standing charges (insurance, depreciation, garage rent) accrue with time; running charges vary with distance or usage.

formulas.name: Transport cost per tonne-km
formulas.expression: Cost per tonne-km = Total operating cost / (Tonnes carried × Kilometres run)
formulas.meaning: Use actual loaded kilometres, and account separately for empty running where the question requires it.
formulas.example: Total cost ₹8,00,000; 500 tonnes × 400 km = 2,00,000 tonne-km → ₹4 per tonne-km.

formulas.name: Cost per passenger-km
formulas.expression: Cost per passenger-km = Total cost / (Passengers × Distance)
formulas.meaning: Where seats are partly occupied, use capacity or effective passenger-km and explain the basis.
formulas.example: 60 seats at 70% occupancy over 200 trips of 50 km → 4,20,000 passenger-km.

pitfalls: Ignoring empty running in the denominator.
Treating driver wages as a fixed standing charge when they are paid per trip.

chapters.summary: Unit and output costing are single-costing methods for homogeneous output. The cost sheet is the main deliverable and includes treatment of scrap, defectives and spoilage.

keyTerms.definition: Cost per unit where a single uniform product is produced, often with a cost sheet.
Residual material with small realisable value; its recovery reduces material cost.
Units that can be rectified and sold; rectification cost is normally charged to the specific job or to production overheads if normal.
Units that cannot be rectified; treated as loss, with any recovery credited.

revisionNotes: Normal defective work is absorbed into overheads; abnormal defective work is charged to the costing P&L.
Cost sheet questions frequently require a tender or quotation — add the required margin on cost or on sales as specified.

chapters.summary: Standard costing compares predetermined costs with actuals and analyses variances. Material, labour, overhead and sales variances must be computed and reconciled, and the variances must then be interpreted — the interpretation carries marks.

keyTerms.definition: A predetermined cost based on technical specifications and efficient operating conditions, used as a benchmark.
Ideal standards assume perfect conditions; attainable standards allow for normal loss and are more useful for motivation.
(Standard price − Actual price) × Actual quantity purchased or used, depending on the convention stated.
Mix variance isolates the effect of using a different input combination; yield variance isolates the effect of different total output from the given input.
(Standard hours for actual output − Actual hours) × Standard rate.
Absorbed fixed overhead − Budgeted fixed overhead, analysed into capacity and efficiency components.
The effect of price and volume differences on contribution or margin, valued at standard margin.

formulas.name: Material cost variance
formulas.expression: MCV = (SQ for actual output × SP) − (AQ × AP) = Price variance + Usage variance
formulas.meaning: Always compute the total first, then reconcile to its components.

formulas.name: Material price variance
formulas.expression: MPV = (SP − AP) × AQ purchased
formulas.meaning: Favourable if the actual price is below standard.

formulas.name: Material usage variance
formulas.expression: MUV = (SQ for actual output − AQ) × SP
formulas.meaning: Favourable if less material was used than allowed.

formulas.name: Material mix variance
formulas.expression: MMV = (Revised standard quantity − Actual quantity) × Standard price, where RSQ = Total AQ × Standard proportion
formulas.meaning: Isolates the effect of deviating from the standard mix.
formulas.example: Total AQ 1,100; standard mix 60:40 → RSQ A 660, B 440.

formulas.name: Labour rate and efficiency variance
formulas.expression: LRV = (SR − AR) × AH; LEV = (SH for actual output − AH) × SR
formulas.meaning: Rate variance is usually the purchasing/HR responsibility; efficiency variance is operational.

formulas.name: Variable overhead variance
formulas.expression: VO cost variance = (Standard hours × Standard VO rate) − Actual VO; split into expenditure and efficiency
formulas.meaning: Expenditure variance = (Standard rate × Actual hours) − Actual VO.
formulas.example: SH 500 × ₹20 = 10,000; AH 480 × ₹20 = 9,600; actual 9,900 → efficiency ₹400 F, expenditure ₹300 A.

formulas.name: Fixed overhead variance
formulas.expression: FO cost variance = Absorbed − Actual; volume variance = Absorbed − Budgeted; expenditure variance = Budgeted − Actual
formulas.meaning: Absorbed = Actual hours × standard FO rate.
formulas.example: Budgeted ₹50,000; absorbed ₹48,000; actual ₹52,000 → expenditure ₹2,000 A; volume ₹2,000 A; total ₹4,000 A.

formulas.name: Sales margin variance
formulas.expression: Sales margin price variance = (Actual price − Standard price) × Actual quantity; sales margin volume variance = (Actual quantity − Budgeted quantity) × Standard margin
formulas.meaning: Use margin, not sales value, when costs vary.
formulas.example: Std margin ₹10/unit; actual 1,100 vs budget 1,000 → volume variance ₹1,000 F.

examples.title: Reconciling variances
examples.scenario: Budget: 1,000 units, 2 kg material at ₹20, 1 hour labour at ₹100. Actual: 1,100 units, 2,150 kg at ₹21, 1,150 hours at ₹98.
steps: Material: SQ for actual output 2,200 kg; MUV = (2,200 − 2,150) × 20 = ₹1,000 F; MPV = (20 − 21) × 2,150 = ₹2,150 A; total ₹1,150 A.
examples.result: Present a reconciliation statement from standard cost of actual output to actual cost, then interpret: the price increase outweighed material efficiency gains, while labour efficiency deteriorated despite a lower rate.

questions.q: Standard: 5 kg at ₹40 per unit. Actual production 1,000 units using 5,200 kg costing ₹2,13,200. Compute material variances.
Explain the possible causes of an unfavourable labour efficiency variance and who is responsible.
questions.answer: Causes: inefficient working or poor supervision, use of inexperienced or substitute labour, machine breakdowns and idle time, poor quality materials causing rework, inaccurate standard setting, and changed methods. Responsibility normally rests with the production manager, but the cause must be established before blame is assigned — material quality is a purchase function issue, and poor standards are a cost-accounting issue. This is why variance analysis must be paired with investigation rather than automatic action.

pitfalls: Mixing purchase-quantity and usage-quantity bases within the same variance schedule without saying so.
Reporting an adverse variance as 'bad' without investigating its cause.
Using budgeted output instead of standard quantity for actual output.

chapters.summary: Budgeting translates plans into quantified expectations. Functional budgets build into the master budget, and a cash budget is the most frequently examined schedule. Flexible budgets separate fixed and variable behaviour.

keyTerms.definition: A quantitative expression of a plan for a defined period, prepared in advance of the period.
The process of comparing actual results with budgets, analysing variances and taking corrective action.
The summary budget comprising the budgeted P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, supported by functional budgets.
A budget recast for the actual level of activity so that comparisons are like-for-like.
Every activity must be justified from zero each period, rather than incrementally from the previous period.
A schedule of expected cash receipts and payments, showing the closing cash balance and any financing requirement.

formulas.name: Production budget
formulas.expression: Production units = Sales units + Closing finished goods − Opening finished goods
formulas.meaning: Drives the material and labour budgets.

formulas.name: Material purchase budget
formulas.expression: Purchases = Production requirement + Closing raw material − Opening raw material
formulas.meaning: Valued at the expected purchase price.

formulas.name: Cash budget closing balance
formulas.expression: Closing cash = Opening cash + Receipts − Payments (± financing)
formulas.meaning: Collections follow the credit policy; state the collection pattern assumptions.

formulas.name: Flexible budget cost
formulas.expression: Total cost = Fixed cost + (Variable rate × Actual activity)
formulas.meaning: Only variable costs flex; fixed costs remain constant within the relevant range.

questions.q: Sales budget 12,000 units; opening finished goods 800; closing finished goods 1,200; each unit needs 3 kg of material; opening raw material 2,000 kg, closing 2,500 kg. Prepare the production and purchase budgets.
questions.answer: Production = 12,000 + 1,200 − 800 = 12,400 units. Material requirement = 37,200 kg. Purchases = 37,200 + 2,500 − 2,000 = 37,700 kg.

questions.q: Explain the behavioural problems of budgeting.
questions.answer: Budgetary slack (deliberately easy targets), participation versus imposed budgets, departmentalism and rivalry over resource allocation, short-termism and cutting discretionary costs such as training and maintenance, resistance to change, and demotivation where variances are used to punish rather than to improve. Mitigation includes participative budgeting, rolling forecasts, separating controllable from uncontrollable items, and using budgets alongside non-financial measures.

pitfalls: Recasting fixed costs in a flexible budget — they do not flex.
Forgetting the opening balance adjustment in the production budget.

chapters.summary: Marginal costing separates variable and fixed costs and focuses on contribution. Profit is a function of contribution minus fixed cost, so volume, price and mix decisions are analysed through the P/V ratio and break-even.

keyTerms.definition: The variable cost of one additional unit, comprising direct material, direct labour and variable overheads.
Sales minus variable cost; the amount available to cover fixed costs and then generate profit.
Contribution divided by sales, expressing the proportion of each sales rupee available to cover fixed costs.
The level of sales at which total contribution equals fixed costs, so there is neither profit nor loss.
Actual sales minus break-even sales; the amount by which sales can fall before a loss arises.
Recovery of both variable and fixed production costs into product cost; required for external reporting.

formulas.name: Contribution
formulas.expression: Contribution = Sales − Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit
formulas.meaning: The central identity of marginal costing.

formulas.name: P/V ratio
formulas.expression: P/V ratio = Contribution / Sales = (Change in contribution / Change in sales) × 100
formulas.meaning: Use the change formula when comparing two periods.

formulas.name: Break-even sales
formulas.expression: BEP (₹) = Fixed cost / P/V ratio; BEP (units) = Fixed cost / Contribution per unit
formulas.meaning: The point of zero profit.
formulas.example: Fixed ₹2,40,000 / 40% = ₹6,00,000; at ₹100 per unit with ₹40 contribution → 6,000 units.

formulas.name: Margin of safety
formulas.expression: MOS = Actual sales − BEP sales; MOS ratio = MOS / Actual sales; Profit = MOS × P/V ratio
formulas.meaning: A high MOS indicates resilience.

formulas.name: Required sales for target profit
formulas.expression: Required sales = (Fixed cost + Target profit) / P/V ratio
formulas.meaning: Used for planning and for 'what-if' questions.

formulas.name: Multi-product break-even
formulas.expression: Composite P/V ratio = Total contribution / Total sales; BEP = Fixed cost / Composite P/V ratio
formulas.meaning: Assumes a constant sales mix; a change in mix changes the BEP.

formulas.name: Profit reconciliation
formulas.expression: Difference in profit = Change in fixed overhead in closing stock − Change in fixed overhead in opening stock
formulas.meaning: Marginal profit exceeds absorption profit when stock increases.
formulas.example: Closing stock carries ₹30,000 fixed overhead and opening stock ₹10,000 → marginal profit is ₹20,000 higher.

examples.title: Absorption vs marginal profit
examples.scenario: Production 10,000 units, sales 8,000 units, variable cost ₹60/unit, fixed production overhead ₹2,00,000, selling price ₹100.
steps: Absorption: fixed overhead per unit = ₹20; cost of sales 8,000 × 80 = ₹6,40,000; sales ₹8,00,000 → profit ₹1,60,000.
Difference ₹40,000 = 2,000 units in closing stock × ₹20 fixed overhead.
examples.result: Absorption profit is higher by the fixed overhead carried in closing stock. This reconciliation is a standard 5-mark requirement.

questions.q: Fixed cost ₹4,50,000; selling price ₹50; variable cost ₹30. Compute BEP in units and value, and the sales required for a profit of ₹1,50,000.
questions.answer: Contribution per unit ₹20; P/V ratio 40%. BEP units = 4,50,000/20 = 22,500 units; BEP value = ₹11,25,000. Required sales for profit ₹1,50,000 = (4,50,000 + 1,50,000)/0.40 = ₹15,00,000 (30,000 units).

questions.q: Explain why profit under absorption costing differs from profit under marginal costing.
questions.answer: The difference arises solely from the treatment of fixed production overhead. Under absorption costing, a portion of fixed production overhead is carried in the valuation of closing stock and released through cost of sales when sold; under marginal costing, the entire fixed cost is charged to the period. Therefore, when stock increases, absorption profit is higher by the fixed overhead in the increase in stock; when stock decreases, absorption profit is lower. When production equals sales, the two profits are identical. The reconciliation quantifies the change in fixed overhead held in stock.

pitfalls: Using total cost instead of variable cost in the contribution.
Forgetting to change the BEP when the sales mix changes in a multi-product question.

formulas.name: Learning curve
formulas.expression: Average time for the first 2n units = Average time for the first n units × Learning rate
formulas.meaning: Applies to labour-intensive, repetitive tasks.
formulas.example: 80% curve: first unit 100 hours; average for 2 units 80; for 4 units 64; total time for 4 units 256 hours.

questions.q: An 80% learning curve applies. The first unit takes 1,000 hours. Compute the total time for 8 units.
questions.answer: Cumulative average: 1 unit 1,000; 2 units 800; 4 units 640; 8 units 512 hours. Total time for 8 units = 8 × 512 = 4,096 hours. The marginal time for units 5–8 is 4,096 − 2,560 = 1,536 hours.
